lead: This unit designs the two members that carry a building down to the ground: columns and footings. You will classify columns, design short columns for axial load and bending, and proportion wall, isolated and combined footings. You will also meet retaining walls and water tanks as applications of the same ideas.
about: The unit moves from the compression member to the foundation. Chapter 5.1 classifies columns and fixes effective length and slenderness. Chapter 5.2 designs an axially loaded short column. Chapter 5.3 adds uniaxial and biaxial bending with interaction diagrams. Chapter 5.4 treats wall footings. Chapter 5.5 designs isolated square, rectangular and circular footings. Chapter 5.6 extends this to a combined footing for two columns. Chapter 5.7 applies the same stability and bending ideas to cantilever retaining walls. Chapter 5.8 closes with water tanks, where liquid pressure and crack control govern. Each chapter uses the limit state method from Unit 1 and the beam design from Unit 2.

chapters.idea: A column is classified by its lateral support and by its slenderness ratio, which decides whether it is designed as short or slender.
chapters.depth: Tied and spiral columns; braced and unbraced columns; effective length from end restraints; slenderness ratio about both axes as effective length divided by the least lateral dimension. A column is short when both ratios are ≤ 12. Minimum eccentricity e_min = l/500 + D/30, with a floor of 20 mm. Some syllabi call the slenderness ratio the column slenderness.

figure.title: Column classification
figure.aria: Flow from column to effective length to slenderness ratios, then to short if both ratios are at most 12 or slender if any ratio is more than 12.

chapters.example: A tied column has section 300 mm × 450 mm and unsupported length 3.6 m. Both ends are pinned in a braced frame. Find the effective length, the slenderness ratios about both axes, and classify the column as short or slender.
chapters.trap: Using the unsupported length instead of the effective length, or checking only the major axis. The 12 limit applies to both axes.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1: limit state philosophy and material behaviour.

chapters.idea: A short column under axial load is designed by choosing longitudinal steel so that the factored load is less than the concrete plus steel capacity, then detailing ties.
chapters.depth: Limit state of collapse in compression. For a tied short column with minimum eccentricity, Pu = 0.4 fck Ac + 0.67 fy Asc. Here Pu is factored axial load in N, fck is concrete cube strength in N/mm², fy is steel yield strength in N/mm², Ac = Ag − Asc is concrete area in mm², Ag is gross area in mm², and Asc is steel area in mm². Steel limits are 0.8% to 6% of Ag. Ties: diameter at least one quarter of the largest bar and not less than 6 mm; spacing not more than the least lateral dimension and not more than 16 times the smallest bar diameter.

figure.title: Axial column design
figure.aria: Design flow from factored load 1200 kN, to steel area, to gross area 300 by 400 mm, to four 20 mm bars, to 8 mm ties at 300 mm spacing.

chapters.example: Design the longitudinal steel and ties for a short tied rectangular column 300 mm × 400 mm carrying a factored axial load of 1200 kN. Use M20 concrete and Fe415 steel. Take cover 40 mm.
chapters.trap: Forgetting Ac = Ag − Asc in the concrete term, or ignoring the minimum steel of 0.8% of Ag.
chapters.leave: Bending and interaction diagrams to 5.3; detailing rules to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A column under axial load plus moment is safe if its load-moment point lies inside the interaction diagram, for one axis or for both axes together.
chapters.depth: Short rectangular and circular columns for uniaxial and biaxial bending. Interaction diagram between factored axial load Pu and factored moment Mu. Key points: pure compression, balanced point, pure bending. Use design charts, such as SP 16. Minimum eccentricity moments are added to calculated moments. For biaxial bending use a load contour check, for example (Mux/Mux1)^αn + (Muy/Muy1)^αn ≤ 1. Here Mux and Muy are applied moments about the two axes, Mux1 and Muy1 are uniaxial moment capacities at the same Pu, and αn is a exponent often taken between 1 and 2. Some syllabi call this the Bresler load contour method.

figure.aria: Interaction curve of axial load against moment; the design point at 90 kN·m and 800 kN lies inside the curve.

chapters.example: A 300 mm × 400 mm short column has 4 bars of 20 mm diameter, M20 concrete and Fe415 steel. It carries Pu = 800 kN, Mux = 90 kN·m and Muy = 40 kN·m. From SP 16 charts, Mux1 = 130 kN·m and Muy1 = 100 kN·m at Pu. Check the section for biaxial bending using αn = 1.5.
chapters.trap: Adding the two moment ratios linearly, or using the first-order moment without the minimum eccentricity moment.
chapters.leave: Slender column second-order effects to 5.1 effective length; detailing to Unit 3.

chapters.idea: A wall footing spreads a wall load over soil, with width from bearing pressure and thickness from bending and shear.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Strip footing under a masonry or concrete wall. Design as a cantilever slab projecting on each side of the wall. Width from service load divided by safe bearing capacity. Factored upward soil pressure. Bending moment at the wall face; one-way shear at a distance d from the wall face. Distribution steel along the length. Minimum thickness and cover. Some syllabi call this a strip footing.

figure.title: Wall footing
figure.aria: Wall footing flow from 180 kN per metre wall load, to 1.2 m width, to 150 kN per square metre soil pressure, to 26.5 kN·m per metre moment, to 200 mm depth.

chapters.example: A 230 mm brick wall carries a service load of 180 kN per metre length. The safe bearing capacity of the soil is 150 kN/m². Design the width and thickness of a wall footing using M20 concrete and Fe415 steel. Take cover 50 mm.
chapters.trap: Using service soil pressure with factored moments, or taking the critical bending section at the footing edge instead of the wall face.
chapters.leave: Isolated footings to 5.5; combined footings to 5.6.

chapters.idea: An isolated footing spreads one column load, is sized by bearing, and is designed for bending, one-way shear and punching shear.
chapters.depth: Axially and eccentrically loaded pad and sloped footings; square, rectangular and circular shapes. Area from service load and safe bearing capacity. Factored net upward pressure. Bending at the column face. One-way shear at a distance d from the column face. Punching shear on a perimeter at d/2 from the column face. Development length of column bars into the footing. Sloped footings save concrete but need shear checks at each critical section.

figure.title: Isolated footing checks
figure.aria: Flow from 400 mm column and 1000 kN load to 5 square metre area, to 2.3 m square footing, then to bending, one-way shear and punching shear checks.

chapters.example: An isolated square footing supports a 400 mm square column with a service load of 1000 kN. The safe bearing capacity is 200 kN/m². Use M20 concrete and Fe415 steel. Find the footing size and the depth required for bending at the column face. Take cover 50 mm.
chapters.trap: Checking punching shear on the column face instead of the perimeter at d/2, or using gross soil pressure with factored loads.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 beams; Unit 3 shear and bond; 5.4 wall footing.
chapters.leave: Combined footings to 5.6; tank base slabs to 5.8.

chapters.idea: A combined footing for two columns is proportioned so its centroid lies under the resultant of the column loads, then designed as a longitudinal beam with transverse bending.
chapters.depth: Rectangular combined footing for two columns only. Total area from sum of service loads and safe bearing capacity. Choose width and length so the footing centroid coincides with the load resultant. Factored upward soil pressure. Longitudinal bending between and beyond columns. Transverse bending under each column. One-way shear and punching shear checks. Some syllabi call this a two-column footing.

figure.title: Combined footing plan
figure.aria: Two column loads 600 kN and 900 kN give a resultant at 1.8 m; the footing centroid is placed at 1.8 m, giving length 5 m and width 2 m.

chapters.example: Two 400 mm square columns carry service loads of 600 kN and 900 kN. Their centre-to-centre spacing is 3 m. The safe bearing capacity is 150 kN/m². Design the plan size of a rectangular combined footing with width 2 m. Check that the centroid of the footing lies under the resultant.
chapters.trap: Placing the footing centroid at mid-length instead of under the load resultant, or ignoring transverse bending under each column.
chapters.leave: Retaining walls to 5.7; water tanks to 5.8.

chapters.idea: A cantilever retaining wall holds back soil with a stem fixed to a base slab, and it must be stable against overturning, sliding and bearing before its parts are designed.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this. Stem, heel, toe and base slab. Active earth pressure with coefficient Ka. Pressure acts as a triangle; total thrust is one half Ka γ H² per metre length, with resultant at H/3 above the base. Here γ is soil unit weight in kN/m³ and H is retained height in m. Stability checks for overturning, sliding and base bearing. Design of stem as a cantilever, and heel and toe as cantilever slabs.

figure.title: Retaining wall
figure.aria: Flow from soil pressure 24 kN per square metre to thrust 48 kN per metre, then to stem, base slab, and heel and toe.

chapters.example: A cantilever retaining wall retains 4 m of soil with unit weight 18 kN/m³ and angle of internal friction 30°. Take Ka = 1/3. Find the active earth pressure at the base and the total thrust per metre length. State the height of the resultant above the base.
chapters.trap: Taking the resultant at half the height instead of one third, or forgetting that the pressure diagram is triangular.
chapters.leave: Water tanks to 5.8; full stability checking practice to design office methods.

chapters.idea: A water tank must be designed for water pressure and for crack control, because leakage and durability govern as much as strength.
chapters.depth: Some syllabi add water tanks as an application. Circular and rectangular tanks. Water pressure p = γw h, where γw is about 10 kN/m³ and h is depth in m. In a circular tank, hoop tension per metre height is T = p r, where r is tank radius in m. In a rectangular tank, walls bend as vertical cantilevers or as panels. Base slab design. Minimum reinforcement and crack width control for liquid tightness. Some syllabi call this liquid-retaining structure design.

figure.title: Circular tank
figure.aria: Flow from 3 m water depth to 30 kN per square metre pressure, to 90 kN per metre hoop tension, to 600 square millimetre per metre steel, to 10 mm bars at 130 mm spacing.

chapters.example: A circular water tank has internal diameter 6 m and water depth 3 m. Find the hoop tension per metre height at the base. Design the hoop steel using a permissible tensile stress of 150 N/mm². Use 10 mm bars.
chapters.trap: Using average water pressure for hoop tension at the base, or designing only for strength and not for crack control.
chapters.prereq: Unit 2 beams and serviceability; Unit 3 detailing.
chapters.leave: Detailed crack-width calculation to Unit 2 serviceability; prestressed tanks to Unit 6.
